batchName: Middle Republic: The Gracchi (133-121 BCE) - Hard Batch 1

questions.question: Why might Tiberius Gracchus have married the daughter of a former consul from a rival family?
options: To fulfil his father's dying wish
To secure his election as quaestor
To acquire large estates of public land
To reconcile the two houses
To escape heavy family debts
To win the support of Egypt
questions.explanation: The marriage was perhaps part of a plan to reconcile two great families. The Gracchi were woven into Rome's leading clans, and their sister married a famous general.
questions.sourceQuote: The brothers' sister married a leading general, and Tiberius married the daughter of a former consul from a rival family, perhaps as part of a plan to reconcile the two houses.

questions.question: Gaius Gracchus's law on citizens' right of appeal drove which man into exile?
options: The consul Opimius
A former consul linked to punishing Tiberius's men
The tribune who had vetoed Tiberius's bill
Scipio Nasica, the chief priest
A governor accused of extortion in Asia
The censor who had questioned Gaius
questions.explanation: The law reaffirmed that a citizen facing death could appeal to the people and declared courts not set up by the people illegal, which caught out a former consul.
questions.sourceQuote: It drove into exile a former consul linked to the punishment of Tiberius Gracchus's supporters.

questions.question: Which sequence of events in 121 BC is in the correct order?
options: Carthage colony challenged, final decree, attendant killed, Aventine stand
Final decree, Carthage colony challenged, attendant killed, Aventine stand
Attendant killed, Carthage colony challenged, Aventine stand, final decree
Attendant killed, final decree, Aventine stand, Carthage colony challenged
Aventine stand, attendant killed, final decree, Carthage colony challenged
Carthage colony challenged, attendant killed, final decree, Aventine stand
questions.explanation: A tribune moved to cancel the Carthage colony, an attendant was killed at a sacrifice, the Senate passed its final decree, and Gaius's followers seized the Aventine. Gaius then fled across the Tiber and died.
questions.sourceQuote: In 121 BC a new tribune moved to cancel the colony at Carthage.

questions.question: Roughly how many settlers could the land distributed by the Gracchan commission have supported?
options: About 1.3 million
About 3,268
questions.explanation: The commission distributed about 3,268 square kilometres (1.3 million jugera). The number of registered citizens rose in the following decade.
questions.sourceQuote: Over a few busy years it distributed some 3,268 square kilometres (1.3 million jugera) of land, enough for somewhere between 70,000 and 130,000 settlers.

questions.question: Why did Tiberius's bid for a second consecutive term as tribune particularly alarm his enemies?
options: Officials in office could not be prosecuted
It would let him appoint the next consuls
Re-elected tribunes became senators for life
Tribunes automatically commanded armies
It would make him chief priest of Rome
It would hand him control of the treasury
questions.explanation: Endless re-election meant endless immunity from prosecution. Historians note that his enemies feared his tactics more than the reform itself.
questions.sourceQuote: This may have been illegal, and it certainly broke custom: officials could not be prosecuted while in office, so endless re-election meant endless immunity.

questions.question: When the censors questioned Gaius Gracchus for leaving Sardinia without permission, how did he defend himself?
options: His commander had ordered him to leave
His mother had summoned him home
The Senate had recalled him to Rome
The harsh winter made duty impossible
He had already served longer than most men
He had fallen seriously ill
questions.explanation: Gaius left when his commander's posting was extended and justified himself by his length of service. He was later elected tribune for 123 BC.
questions.sourceQuote: Questioned by the censors, he argued he had already served longer than most men.

questions.question: What became of Scipio Nasica after he was charged with Tiberius Gracchus's murder?
options: He was exiled to Spain for life
He retired quietly to Campania
He was acquitted and elected consul
He was convicted and executed
He was sent to Pergamum and died there
He was made censor the next year
questions.explanation: Nasica was conveniently sent on a mission to Pergamum, where he died the next year. Tiberius's killing was unprecedented in Roman politics.
questions.sourceQuote: Afterwards Scipio Nasica was charged with murder, but was sent on a convenient mission to Pergamum, where he died the next year.

questions.question: Who supported Tiberius Gracchus's land bill in 133 BC? (select all that apply)
options: The leaders of the Italian allies
Most of the landholding elite
Some senators
One of that year's consuls
The chief priest Scipio Nasica
Country people who flocked to Rome
questions.explanation: Country people poured into Rome to back Tiberius, and some senators and one consul supported the bill. Most of the elite, who held large amounts of public land, opposed it.
questions.sourceQuote: Many in the elite, who held large amounts of public land, fought the bill hard, though some senators and one of that year's consuls backed it.

questions.question: What happened to the consul after Rome rejected the treaty Tiberius negotiated at Numantia?
options: He was fined heavily but kept his rank
He was granted a minor triumph
He was demoted to quaestor
He was exiled to Massilia
He was executed in the Forum
He was stripped of citizenship and handed over bound
questions.explanation: The consul was handed to the Numantines naked and bound. A proposal to send Tiberius in chains with him was defeated.
questions.sourceQuote: The consul was stripped of his citizenship and handed over to the Numantines naked and bound.

questions.question: When and why was the Gracchan land commission finally closed?
options: In 91 BC, at the start of the Social War
In 111 BC, after it was declared illegal
In 133 BC, after Tiberius's murder
In 121 BC, by Opimius's special court
In 129 BC, after the Italian protests
In 111 BC, once its work was done
questions.explanation: Oddly, most of Gaius's laws survived his death. The grain law lasted until the last decade of the century.
questions.sourceQuote: The grain law lasted until the last decade of the century, and the land commission was closed only in 111 BC, once its work was done.
